title: Net Trap Camera Workflow: Placement and Boar Blanket Coordination
content:
Net traps are passive by nature. Hogs slide under an elevated net during conditioning, then you drop when the full sounder is present. Without live visibility, that drop happens on guesswork or a drive to the site that educates the group before you ever send the closure command.

A net trap camera workflow turns that passive setup into an active trap program. This guide covers camera placement for net trap sites, the conditioning-to-catch switch you make from the app, and light coordination with a Boar Blanket net system so monitoring drives the drop, not the calendar.

Why a Net Trap Camera Workflow Starts With the Decision Zone

Net trap success depends on two decisions: when hogs are fully conditioned to feed under the net, and when the complete sounder is present for the drop. Both require seeing the bait zone clearly, not a corner of the frame where a single hog crossed at midnight.

Unlike standard trail cameras designed for wildlife observation, a wild hog trap camera system delivers continuous live video and remote closure control. The net trap camera workflow is built around that feed: count hogs, read commitment, switch from conditioning to catch phase remotely, then drop when criteria are met.

Partial drops educate survivors. Trap-shy hogs set a site back for months. Whole-sounder removal is the only approach with lasting results on net trap sites, and that starts with monitoring multiple nights to know sounder size before you trigger.

Camera Placement for Net Trap Sites

Placement on net trap sites differs from corral traps because the decision zone is wider and the net geometry matters as much as the bait pile.

  1. Frame bait and net perimeter together. You need to see hogs sliding under the elevated net during conditioning and confirm the full group is under the net footprint before drop.
  2. Cover entry paths, not just the bait pile. Sounders often circle before they commit. Edge motion is not the same as a group inside the net zone.
  3. Mount for height without losing the under-net view. Net traps often sit on open pasture or tree-set timber. Angle down enough to read hog count, but keep enough sky in the antenna path for cellular reporting.
  4. Test from the final mount point. Confirm reports and live view quality from where the camera will live, not from the truck on the road.

Conditioning Phase: What the Camera Confirms

During conditioning, the net stays elevated on T-posts roughly 7 to 10 feet so hogs slide under and feel the net without obstruction. The camera job in this phase is observation, not trigger:

  • Confirm hogs are returning on a predictable schedule.
  • Count how many animals are in the sounder across multiple nights.
  • Verify bait never runs out. Empty bait stops conditioning and resets trust.
  • Watch for trap-shy behavior: circling without entering, sudden stops after a partial event elsewhere on the property.

Monitor multiple days before you treat the site as catch-ready. Summer sounders cluster near water and wallows. If no natural water is nearby, a mud hole with buckets can hold a group on bait longer, and the camera tells you whether that tactic is working.

Boar Blanket Coordination Without a Trap-Type Deep Dive

HogEye works with any trap, including soft net systems. The Boar Blanket is HogEye's soft net option for large sounder capture on open or tree-set sites. The coordination point is monitoring, not net rigging specs.

When you run a Boar Blanket with HogEye, the workflow stays consistent:

  • Pre-bait and elevate the net in conditioning mode.
  • Watch live video to count the sounder and confirm bait discipline.
  • Switch from conditioning to catch phase remotely when the full sounder is present.
  • Send the closure command from the app to drop the net when criteria are met.

You do not need to drive to the site to flip modes or guess whether the group is under the net. That is the active net trap advantage HogEye adds to a system that is otherwise passive until someone visits the bait hub.

Catch Phase: Remote Drop Readiness Checklist

Before you send the closure command on a net trap site, run the same readiness checklist every time:

  • Camera health. Unit reporting, power stable, live view clear.
  • Trap status. Net in catch configuration, not still elevated in conditioning mode.
  • Sounder count. Full group accounted for across recent nights, not just the first hogs through.
  • Bait holding. Group settled and feeding, not circling the edge.
  • Closure criteria met. Whole sounder inside the net footprint and settled.

Trigger when the whole sounder is inside and settled. Do not drop on the first hogs under the net. Review wild hog behavior and trap timing before you trust early entries as a drop signal.

A purpose-built HogEye camera integrates with net trap actuators for remote closure. Digital pan, tilt, and zoom let you refine the view after install when hogs shift how they enter under the net.

Net Trap Workflow vs. Trail Camera Alerts

The 90-second problem applies directly to net traps. By the time a trail cam photo arrives, the sounder may have fed and left. Net drops are one high-consequence decision. Missing the window or dropping too early both educate the group.

Continuous live video, motion context, and one-touch remote trigger from the HogEye app are what make net trap programs consistent. Compare approaches in the hog trapping cameras compared piece if your team is still splitting attention between scouting cams and trap closure.

Power and Reporting on Remote Net Trap Sites

Net trap sites often sit on open pasture with good solar exposure, but tree-set layouts in timber need the same uptime discipline as corral traps on trap lines. Angle the panel toward open sky, confirm reporting after rain, and recheck mounts when livestock or wind shift the rigging. Dispatch and Reset: What the Camera Confirms After Drop

After a successful net drop, the camera still has a job. Confirm the sounder is contained under the net footprint, plan dispatch and safe removal, and verify bait and rigging status before you reset for the next cycle. Operators who leave net trap sites unmonitored after capture miss early signs that survivors are testing the edge or that rigging shifted during dispatch activity.

Net trap mesh and rigging wear with use. Budget repairs and eventual replacement material as part of the long-term program cost. Monitoring through reset and conditioning on the next bait hub protects the timeline you built on the first capture.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where should I mount a camera on a net trap site?

Frame bait and net perimeter together, cover entry paths, and confirm you can count hogs under the elevated net during conditioning and under the net footprint before drop.

How does HogEye coordinate with a Boar Blanket net trap?

HogEye provides live video and remote closure control. You watch conditioning, switch to catch phase remotely, and send the drop command from the app when the full sounder is present.

Can I run a net trap without a monitoring camera?

You can, but results are inconsistent. Net drops are one high-consequence decision. Without live visibility, operators miss the window or drop too early, both of which educate the sounder.

How long should I monitor before dropping a net?

Monitor multiple nights to count sounder size and confirm predictable returns. Conditioning often runs 14 to 21 days before catch phase, with bait never running out during that window.

What is the difference between conditioning and catch phase on a net trap?

Conditioning keeps the net elevated so hogs slide under freely. Catch phase lowers the net into position so the next visit can contain the full sounder when you send the closure command remotely.
